question: When do those Signals run, and can they stop a bad answer before the user sees it?

observer.firstAnswerText:
Signals run after an agent turn has finished. A turn is one exchange between the user and the agent. Because the turn is already over when scoring starts, Signals can't stop a bad answer before the user sees it. They help you find problems after the fact. To block or change a response before it reaches the user, you need a guardrail in your application code.

When Signals run

When a turn's root span ends, Weave treats the turn as complete. (The root span is the top-level record of the turn; it has no parent.) Weave then emits a weave.genai.turn_ended event. A background scoring worker loads the project's active signals, applies each signal's filters and sample rate, scores the turn, and saves the result as feedback on that turn [S17].
Weave scores only completed turns, not individual LLM calls or tool calls [S17]. The Signals table shows only turn as the scored type, and its When column shows when each signal was scored [S14].
You can limit which turns a signal scores with filters, such as by agent, tool or model. You can also set a sample rate so it scores only some of the matching turns, which lowers cost on busy agents [S16]. You can turn a signal on or off at any time [S13].
If you score turns with your own HTTP endpoint (a remote scorer), Weave retries failed requests up to three attempts within 30 seconds [S17].

Why Signals can't block answers (my inference) Signals score a turn only after it has ended, and they record the result as feedback. So the answer has already been produced by the time a signal flags it. Signals flag problems and highlight traces that need your attention [S1].

If you need to stop bad answers

Weave guardrails run in real time, before outputs reach users. They can block or modify responses when a score crosses a threshold [S10].
Guardrails use inline Weave Scorers and require code changes, because they change how your application runs. Their scores are also stored in Weave, so they double as monitoring [S12].
The Weave TypeScript SDK doesn't support the tools needed to set up guardrails [S12].
The guardrails guide is written around LLM apps rather than the Agents view, so check that guide before wiring a guardrail into your agent.

A common setup is to use guardrails for anything that must never reach users, and Signals to watch quality trends after the fact.
